text.p: Ministers of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum said on Saturday they had made a "credible beginning" towards creating the world's biggest free trade zone but warned against complacency.

A joint ministerial statement at the end of a two-day meeting in Manila was vague about the outcome of discussions on a U.S.-proposed common APEC stance on information technology products such as computers.

Washington, with Japanese backing, had wanted APEC to join it in pushing for tariff-free trade by the year 2000 in computers and other info-tech products at next month's World Trade Organisation summit in Singapore.
Malaysia led opposition to the plan, which was supposed to have been one of the main fruits of this year's annual APEC gatherings.
Saturday's statement said the ministers simply endorsed efforts to arrive at an agreement on the issue.

The trade and foreign ministers who met in Manila as a prelude to the APEC leaders' summit on Monday also endorsed an expanded role for the private sector in APEC and committed the grouping to find ways to spread the booming region's wealth more equitably.
But it quoted Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda as warning "ministers not to fall into complacency".
"APEC is to be maintained as a dynamic evolving process... to show the world that the APEC process is worthy of great credibility," he said.

Critics argue that APEC's voluntary approach means it lacks the teeth to ensure its members meet their commitments to lower all trade barriers in the region by 2010 for developed members and 2020 for the less well off.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
